facts.raw_span: recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol
symptoms persisting for 2 years but worsening on admission
symptoms usually occurred 6-20 hours after alcohol ingestion and lasted 5-10 minutes
syncope occurred only after large alcohol intake
hypertension diagnosed 3 months prior
smoking and alcohol overconsumption (250g/week) for about 20 years
No specific physical examination findings were documented in the case report
High-sensitivity troponin I: 0.01 ng/mL (normal)
Serum potassium: 4.6 mEq/L (normal)
High-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions
ST segments elevated 4-6 mm in leads II, III and aVF, with ST depression in leads V2-V6
10% stenosis in proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) and right coronary artery (RCA)

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms of recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol, along with the ECG findings of high-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions, suggest alcoholic cardiomyopathy.
The patient's history of hypertension diagnosed 3 months prior, combined with the ECG findings, supports the diagnosis of hypertensive heart disease.

The patient's ECG findings and coronary angiography results showing 10% stenosis in the proximal left anterior descending artery and right coronary artery support the diagnosis of coronary artery disease.
The patient's symptoms of syncope after large alcohol intake, along with the ECG findings of premature ventricular contractions, suggest alcohol-induced arrhythmia.

rationales.F01: The presence of recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol suggests a possible link to alcohol consumption, which is a key factor in Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy and Alcohol-induced Arrhythmia.
rationales.F04: Syncope occurring only after large alcohol intake may indicate an arrhythmic cause, which is more closely related to Alcohol-induced Arrhythmia.
rationales.F06: Long-term smoking and alcohol overconsumption are risk factors for multiple cardiovascular conditions, including Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy, Hypertensive Heart Disease, and Coronary Artery Disease, but are most strongly associated with Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy and Alcohol-induced Arrhythmia.
rationales.F10: High-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions are indicative of significant cardiac conduction abnormalities, which can be seen in both Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy and Alcohol-induced Arrhythmia.
rationales.F12: The presence of only mild stenosis in the coronary arteries makes Coronary Artery Disease a less likely primary diagnosis, and also reduces the likelihood of Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy being secondary to coronary disease.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's long history of excessive alcohol consumption and symptoms triggered by alcohol intake, such as recurrent abdominal pain and syncope, support Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy as the most fitting diagnosis.
